Key Takeaways The Russian Ministry of Defense (MoD) continues to greatly exaggerate the extent of Russian advances across the frontline to construct a false narrative of Russian battlefield progress for domestic and international audiences. The unusual MoD statement comes in the midst of Russian State Duma elections and shortly before the convening of the United Nations General Assembly in New York. * The Russian MoD also tried to deny Ukrainian successes in the Lyman direction by presenting an inaccurate picture of the battlefield that denies the ample evidence provided by Russian milbloggers, Ukrainian sources, and geolocated footage. * The Russian MoD’s claims likely aim to shape Russian voters’ perceptions of the war during the ongoing State Duma elections as well as the perceptions of foreign governments that support Ukraine. * Ukrainian forces extensively targeted Russian drone operators as part of their battlefield-shaping effort that enabled Ukrainian drone overmatch prior to Ukraine’s Operation Vivaldi in the Lyman direction. * The US Department of State approved on September 18 the sale of air defense equipment worth $2.68 billion to Ukraine. * US President Donald Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act on September 18. * Ukrainian forces recently advanced in the eastern Fortress Belt and Oleksandrivka directions, while Russian forces recently advanced in the southern Fortress Belt direction. * Russia launched two Zirkon anti-ship missiles and 174 drones and loitering munitions at Ukraine overnight. Russian forces conducted a series of missile and drone strikes against Ukraine on the night of September 18 to 19. The Ukrainian Air Force reported that Russian forces launched two Zirkon anti-ship missiles from Kursk Oblast and 174 Shahed-type strike drones (about half of which were jet-powered), Gerbera-type strike drones, Banderol/Dan-T loitering munitions, and Parodiya-type decoy drones from the directions of Oryol City; Millerovo, Rostov Oblast; Primorsko-Akhtarsk, Krasnodar Krai; occupied Donetsk City; and occupied Hvardiiske, Crimea.[48] The Ukrainian Air Force reported that Russian forces mainly targeted Odesa and Kyiv oblasts; that Ukrainian forces downed 141 air targets, including three Banderol/Dan-T loitering munitions and 138 drones; that an unspecified number of air targets hit 15 locations; and that debris fell at nine locations. The Ukrainian Air Force clarified that an unspecified number of missiles did not reach their targets. Ukrainian officials reported that Russian forces struck medical, industrial, business, and administrative infrastructure in Dnipropetrovsk, Khmelnytskyi, Kyiv, and Odesa oblasts and conducted a “double tap” strike against rescue workers in Odesa City.[49] The Russian MoD claimed that Russian forces struck logistics centers in Kyiv and Odesa oblasts; dry cargo ships and tanker-type vessels in the Chornomorsk and Odesa City ports; and a launch command post at Voznesensk Air Base in Mykolaiv Oblast.[50] Ukraine’s largest energy company, DTEK, reported on September 19 that over 178,000 families were without power in Odesa Oblast after large-scale Russian strikes on the region.[51] Russian forces conducted a Banderol strike against civilian infrastructure in Balakliya, Kharkiv Oblast on the morning of September 19.[52] Russian forces also conducted a strike against a shopping center in Dnipro City on the afternoon of September 19, and various Russian milbloggers claimed that Russian forces used a ballistic missile, a Dan-T loitering munition, or Geran-type drones for the strike.[53] Russian forces likely continue to target bridges in Odesa Oblast that Ukraine has been using as alternative export routes in the face of Russia’s strike campaign against Ukraine’s Black Sea ports. The Russian MoD claimed that Russian forces struck a pontoon crossing over the Dnister River connecting the Izmail Port in Odesa Oblast to Romania overnight on September 18 to 19.[54] A Russian milblogger claimed that Russian forces struck a bridge across the Dnister near Mayaki, Odesa Oblast (east of Izmail) with about 15 Banderol/Dan-T loitering munitions and five glide bombs.[55] It is unclear if the milblogger is referring to the same reported strike as the Russian MoD. The Ukrainian defense industrial base continues to make progress toward developing and deploying interceptors capable of downing faster jet-powered Russian drones. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky posted footage on September 19 showing a Ukrainian interceptor drone downing a Russian jet-powered Geran-5 drone.[56] Ukrainian drone manufacturer Wild Hornets reported that one of its Ukrainian Sting S interceptor drones also successfully intercepted a Russian jet drone.[57] Zelensky reported that this was the second successful deployment of a new Ukrainian interceptor drone against Russian jet-powered drones.[58] Russian forces have been increasingly leveraging repurposed S-400 missiles to compensate for shortfalls in ballistic missile stockpiles, as ISW previously assessed.[59] Russian forces significantly increased their use of RM48U missiles – repurposed training missiles for S-400 air defense systems that fly on ballistic trajectories at high speeds – during the summer, according to official Ukrainian data that Reuters observed.[60] Russian forces launched two to 15 RM48U missiles between January and June 2026 before launching 87 in July — 55 percent of the total 158 ballistic and hypersonic missiles Russian forces launched in July. The number of Russian-launched Iskander missiles fell to 38 in July and August, down from more than 100 in June 2026, according to Ukraine’s General Prosecutor’s Office. The RM48U reportedly deviates about 300 meters on average from its intended target, which has likely caused higher civilian casualties in the last few months. Ukraine’s systematic intermediate-range strike campaign against Russian logistics in occupied Luhansk Oblast disrupted Russian logistics up to 120 kilometers from the frontline and degraded fuel supplies to the frontline, straining Russia’s ability to use drones and EW to protect against Ukrainian drones.[9] ISW assessed in 2024 that the restoration of operational-level maneuver would require neutralizing the Russian tactical reconnaissance strike complex (TRSC) to facilitate a penetration that Ukrainian forces can exploit, sustainment of these exploitations, and expansion of the campaign design to encompass planning and preparation for successive operations.[10] The TRSC is the expression ISW uses to describe the current system of persistent reconnaissance and strike drones coupled with legacy crewed weapons, artillery, and prepared defenses in depth. Ukrainian forces have successfully incorporated operational planning and battlefield shaping along with achieving surprise by concealing the intent of forces concentrated ostensibly for defensive operations into their offensive template. The Ukrainian mid-range strike campaign isolated Russian frontline forces from reinforcements and supplies. Ukrainian forces established an anti-drone bubble primarily using electronic warfare systems over Ukrainian forces that temporarily disrupted the Russian TRSC and moved with advancing Ukrainian forces. This campaign design is consistent with ISW’s 2024 assessment of how maneuver could be restored in contemporary war. The US Department of State approved on September 18 the sale of air defense equipment worth $2.68 billion to Ukraine.[11] The sale will provide Ukraine with S-300 Clone missiles, GAM-67 missiles, Range-Extended Air Defense Laser Guided Rocket missile systems, several launch systems, RPS 202 counter-unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) radars, and logistical and maintenance support. European contributions and US Foreign Military Financing (FMF), which provides grants and loans to foreign governments to fund the purchase of American defense equipment, will finance the sale if the states conclude the proposed purchases.
